If you define philosophy as scholasticism, perhaps you're right. However, deep thought is equally about asking questions and doubt as it is seeking answers and how they are found. The fundamental basis of philosophical inquiry, like the Socratic method, or logical reasoning, are what need be taught. Evidently to philosophers as well as children, at times.

I agree but again, we're dealing with the minds of children which was originally my point. We should teach children to harbor doubt but philosophy is broad. One would be hard pressed to know where to start when establishing a base. Teaching a child is another beast. I wouldn't set a rubix cube down and expect a child to solve it without understanding the fundamentals of algorithms. This leads to your final point, it isnt if it should be but how should we approach such a task.

I think most children are able to understand fairly complex philosophical ideas if they're around seven or older (no studies to back that up, but I was certainly capable of understanding much of what I study now by the age of seven, and I like to extend that courtesy to other people). I wish we would teach children at least the basics of philosophy, and they certainly should be taught formal ethics. A logic class wouldn't hurt either.

Matthew Lipman's project on Philosophy for children says yes. If I remember correctly, one way to do it is asking the right questions regarding ethical decisions on particular situations that children encounter. There are many other approaches that Lipman describes in his book which I cannot do justice to in this thread. But now to answer your question, I believe so. Children are surprisingly capable of reflecting on the hard questions that lead from why Sally should be punished for hitting Bob and why Doug and Steve can't both be captains, to questions of ethical foundations and social contracts.

If they're young kids you can set them up for the Western philosophical tradition by reading them Greek myths. A little older and (in my experience) they'll think about things if you show them interesting ideas, they tend to not enjoy names unless you give them a picture too. My boy said about Sartre; "He looks like an alien frog mutant."
